<reason>PRO won the central clash. Its "level, not change" reframe of the per-100g label turned CON's strongest opening point ("the disclosure is already there") into a liability, and the "was £2.00, now £1.50" observation showed that delta framing is something retailers already know gets read—so CON's inattention argument became PRO's "manufactured salience" argument. PRO also answered CON's sharpest pressure question cleanly: the baseline is the weight-change event, so promotions cannot blank the flag. CON's best material was the substitution argument (alarm on the auditable door pushes traffic to palm-oil swaps) and its exploitation of PRO's careless "resets expectations honestly" concession on relaunches, which kept a genuine route alive. But CON undercut itself by conceding a headline price rise is visible while calling it "no gain"—nudging cost recovery onto the visible route is exactly the benefit PRO claimed—and its stigma explanation for manufacturer lobbying was only a partial answer to why firms fight a sticker nobody supposedly reads. CON's "sideways not backwards" comparison was rhetorically strong but never squarely met PRO's point that the industry itself deploys deltas whenever they flatter. Both sides were clipped in Rebuttal 2 and both used proper Q/A formatting. Competitive, but PRO made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Rebuttal 2 ([B4.1]): answering CON's baseline pressure question by making the trigger the weight-change event rather than a date, so a rolling promotion cannot reset it—this neutralized CON's most concrete compliance/loophole attack in one move, and paired with the was/now salience point it flipped the "shoppers ignore the label" argument.</best_rebuttal>
